title: Undoing a derivative: antiderivatives and the fundamental theorem

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
An antiderivative of a function f is a function F whose derivative is f, so that dF/dt = f(t).

Each of these is checked by differentiating back, with the rules of section 3 and section 4:

the function f(t) an antiderivative F(t)
a constant c c times t
t(n), for n a whole number t(n plus 1) divided by (n plus 1)
e(kt), for k not zero e(kt) divided by k

Sums and constant multiples are done term by term.

The fundamental theorem of calculus, in the part called the evaluation theorem, says this. If f is continuous from a to b (its graph has no jumps; every rate in this book is) and F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ from a to b of f(t) dt = F(b) minus F(a).

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
section 5 worked out integrals from shapes: rectangles, triangles, trapeziums. That works only for a rate that is steady or changes in a straight line. Most rates bend. This section gives a way that does not need a shape.

Given a rate, find a function whose rate it is. That function is called an antiderivative.

Say the rate is 2t. Which function has the rate 2t? The power rule says t2 does. So t2 is an antiderivative of 2t.

So is t2 plus 5, and t2 plus any fixed number. A fixed number has a rate of zero, so adding one changes nothing about the rate. That is why an antiderivative is written with plus C on the end, where C is any constant.

You never have to trust an antiderivative. Differentiate it and see whether the rate comes back.

the rate an antiderivative
a steady rate c c times t
t(n), n a whole number t(n plus 1) divided by (n plus 1)
e(kt) e(kt) divided by k

The fundamental theorem of calculus says an integral is the antiderivative at the end minus the antiderivative at the start.

∫ from a to b of f(t) dt = F(b) minus F(a)

Here F is any antiderivative of f. The C cancels, because it is added at both ends and then subtracted. So leave it out when you work out an integral.

blocks.alt: Two identical rising curves from t = 0 to 3, one 5 above the other: 0, 1, 4 and 9, and 5, 6, 9 and 14. At t = 2 each has a straight tangent line, and the two tangents are parallel.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Hall and colleagues model a man who cuts his intake by 2 megajoules a day, which is 480 kilocalories a day (Lancet 2011). Keep the deficit at 2 megajoules a day, as the static rule of Book 1, section 7 does. Then one year of it is a rectangle.

2 times 365 = 730

So a deficit of 2 megajoules a day is 730 megajoules a year.

His expenditure falls as his weight falls, so his real deficit shrinks. Suppose, to see the arithmetic, that it halves every year. This shape is made up here, and it is not the paper’s model. A half-time of 1 year means k = 0.693 per year (section 4). With t in years, the deficit in megajoules a year is this.

D(t) = 730 e(-0.693t)

The rate of 730 e(-0.693t) is -0.693 times 730 e(-0.693t). That is not the deficit. It is -0.693 times the deficit. So divide by -0.693 to cancel that factor.

730 divided by 0.693 = 1053.4
F(t) = -1053.4 e(-0.693t)

Check it: differentiate F and see whether 730 e(-0.693t) comes back. The rate of F is -0.693 times -1053.4 e(-0.693t), which is 730 e(-0.693t). Now work out F(1) minus F(0) on your calculator. e(-0.693) is 0.5001, and e0 is 1.

F(1) minus F(0) = -1053.4 times 0.5001 plus 1053.4
1053.4 times (1 minus 0.5001) = 1053.4 times 0.4999
1053.4 times 0.4999 = 526.6

About 526.6 megajoules in the first year, against 730 for the steady deficit.

Take the total up to any later time T. It is F(T) minus F(0), which is 1053.4 times (1 minus e(-0.693T)). As T grows, e(-0.693T) shrinks towards zero, so the total creeps up towards 1053.4 megajoules and never passes it.

A deficit that shrinks adds up to less.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Every total here is energy, in megajoules. Turning it into kilograms needs to know what tissue was lost (Book 1, section 2).

points.html: Check every antiderivative by differentiating it. If the rate you started with does not come back, the antiderivative is wrong, however reasonable it looks. It takes one line.

The antiderivative of e(kt) is e(kt) divided by k, not e(kt). Dropping the k gives the wrong size. For a shrinking curve, e(-kt), dropping the k also gives the wrong sign: the antiderivative is e(-kt) divided by -k.

“The deficit never quite reaches zero, so the loss keeps going for ever” is wrong as arithmetic. A deficit D0 e(-kt), where D0 is its value at the start, adds up to at most D0 divided by k, however long it runs.
These rules cover steady rates, whole-number powers of t, e(kt), and sums and multiples of them. When no antiderivative is at hand, go back to rectangles and bound the error as Book 0, C8 does.

A figure made by multiplying a daily deficit by 365, and then by a number of years, is a steady-deficit total. Any deficit that shrinks adds up to less. In a committee, call such a figure an upper limit, reached only if the deficit never shrinks.
Take F at the upper limit minus F at the lower limit, in that order. The reverse gives the right size with the wrong sign.

blocks.prompt: A deficit shrinks as D(t) = D0 e(-kt), where D0 is its size at t = 0 and k is above zero. Derive the total from t = 0 to t = T. Write beside each line the move you made. Then say what the total approaches as T grows, and why.
blocks.answer:
Find an antiderivative, check it, then take the end minus the start.

F(t) = D0 e(-kt) divided by -k    (the rule for e(kt), with -k in place of k)
the rate of F = -k times D0 e(-kt) divided by -k = D0 e(-kt)    (check by differentiating back)
total = F(T) minus F(0)    (the fundamental theorem)
F(0) = D0 divided by -k    (e0 is 1)
total = D0 e(-kT) divided by -k minus D0 divided by -k    (substitute)
total = D0 times (1 minus e(-kT)) divided by k    (multiply top and bottom by -1 and collect)

As T grows, e(-kT) shrinks towards zero. So 1 minus e(-kT) climbs towards 1, and the total climbs towards D0 divided by k. It never gets there and never passes it.

For example, take D0 = 730 and k = 0.693, as in the illustration.

730 divided by 0.693 = 1053.4

The total over all time is at most 1053.4, however long the deficit runs.

blocks.prompt: Write an antiderivative of each: 6, 4t, 3 t2, and t3 plus 2t. Check each by differentiating it.
blocks.answer:
Use the table’s rules term by term.

6 gives 6t
4t gives 4 times t2 divided by 2, which is 2 t2
3 t2 gives 3 times t3 divided by 3, which is t3
t3 plus 2t gives t4 divided by 4 plus t2

Now differentiate each back with the power rule.

the rate of 6t is 6
the rate of 2 t2 is 2 times 2t, which is 4t
the rate of t3 is 3 t2
the rate of t4 divided by 4 plus t2 is t3 plus 2t

Each rate comes back. Any of these plus a constant would do as well.

blocks.prompt: Work out ∫ from 1 to 3 of 3 t2 dt.
blocks.answer:
An antiderivative of 3 t2 is t3. Take it at the upper limit minus the lower limit.

33 = 27
13 = 1
27 minus 1 = 26

The integral is 26.

blocks.prompt: Work out ∫ from 0 to 2 of e(3t) dt, to two decimal places.
blocks.answer:
An antiderivative of e(3t) is e(3t) divided by 3. At t = 2 the exponent is 6. At t = 0 it is 0, and e0 is 1.

On the calculator, e6 is 403.43. Take the antiderivative at 2 minus the antiderivative at 0.

403.43 divided by 3 minus 1 divided by 3 = (403.43 minus 1) divided by 3
403.43 minus 1 = 402.43
402.43 divided by 3 = 134.14

The integral is 134.14.

blocks.prompt: Work out ∫ from 0 to 4 of 10 e(-0.5t) dt, to two decimal places.
blocks.answer:
An antiderivative of 10 e(-0.5t) is 10 e(-0.5t) divided by -0.5, which is -20 e(-0.5t). Check: its rate is -0.5 times -20 e(-0.5t), which is 10 e(-0.5t).

At t = 4 the exponent is -2. At t = 0, e0 is 1.

e(-2) = 0.1353
-20 times 0.1353 = -2.706
-20 times 1 = -20
-2.706 minus -20 = 17.294

The integral is about 17.29.

blocks.prompt: Work out ∫ from 2 to 5 of 2t dt twice: once with the antiderivative t2, and once with t2 plus 5. Say what happened to the 5.
blocks.answer:
With t2:

52 = 25
22 = 4
25 minus 4 = 21

With t2 plus 5:

25 plus 5 = 30
4 plus 5 = 9
30 minus 9 = 21

Both give 21. The 5 is added at the upper limit and again at the lower limit, and the subtraction takes it away. That is why the plus C is left out when you work out an integral between two limits.

blocks.prompt: A rate is 10 e(-0.5t). Work out its total from t = 0 onwards, over all time. Then work out how long it takes to add up to 95% of that.
blocks.answer:
The total from 0 to T is 10 times (1 minus e(-0.5T)) divided by 0.5. As T grows, e(-0.5T) shrinks towards zero.

10 divided by 0.5 = 20

Over all time the total approaches 20.

It reaches 95% of 20 when 1 minus e(-0.5T) is 0.95. That is when e(-0.5T) is 0.05, which is one twentieth. From section 4, that happens at ln 20 divided by k.

2.996 divided by 0.5 = 5.992

At about T = 5.99.

blocks.prompt: Hall and colleagues (Lancet 2011) model a cut in intake of 480 kilocalories a day. Suppose a person’s net deficit starts at 480 and falls by 0.5 kilocalories a day every day. That fall is made up for this problem. Use an antiderivative to work out the total deficit over 200 days. Then check it with the trapezium.
blocks.answer:
The deficit is 480 minus 0.5t, with t in days. Take it term by term.

0.5 divided by 2 = 0.25
F(t) = 480t minus 0.25 t2

Check: the rate of F is 480 minus 2 times 0.25t, which is 480 minus 0.5t. Now F at 200 minus F at 0. F at 0 is 0.

480 times 200 = 96000
200 times 200 = 40000
0.25 times 40000 = 10000
96000 minus 10000 = 86000

The total deficit is 86,000 kilocalories.

Check with the trapezium. On day 200 the deficit is 480 minus 100, which is 380.

480 plus 380 = 860
860 divided by 2 = 430
430 times 200 = 86000

The same 86,000 kilocalories.

blocks.prompt: Take the same deficit of 480 kilocalories a day (Lancet 2011). Over the first 90 days, compare two totals. In the first, the deficit holds steady. In the second, it halves every 365 days, which is made up for this problem. Give the second as a share of the first.
blocks.answer:
Steady: a rectangle.

480 times 90 = 43200

Halving every 365 days: the rate constant is ln 2 divided by 365, per day.

0.693 divided by 365 = 0.001899
0.001899 times 90 = 0.1709

On the calculator, e(-0.1709) is 0.8429. The total is 480 times (1 minus 0.8429) divided by 0.001899.

1 minus 0.8429 = 0.1571
480 times 0.1571 = 75.408
75.408 divided by 0.001899 = 39709.3

About 39,700 kilocalories.

39709.3 divided by 43200 = 0.919

The halving deficit gives about 92% of the steady one over 90 days. Over three months the shrinking hardly shows. It grows with time, which is why a rule tested only in the first weeks can look better than it is.

blocks.prompt: A deficit shrinks as D0 e(-0.693t), with t in years, so it halves every year. Over the first year it adds up to 400 megajoules. Work out D0, in megajoules a year and then in megajoules a day.
blocks.answer:
Run the total backwards. Over the first year the total is D0 times (1 minus e(-0.693)) divided by 0.693. On the calculator, e(-0.693) is 0.5001, so the bracket is 0.4999.

D0 times 0.4999 divided by 0.693 = 400

Multiply both sides by 0.693, then divide both sides by 0.4999.

400 times 0.693 = 277.2
277.2 divided by 0.4999 = 554.5

D0 is about 554.5 megajoules a year. Divide by 365 for a daily figure.

554.5 divided by 365 = 1.519

About 1.52 megajoules a day at the start.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

∫ from 0 to 3 of (12 minus 2t) dt
an antiderivative is F(t) = 12t minus t2
the integral = F(0) minus F(3)
F(0) = 0 and F(3) = 36 minus 9 = 27
0 minus 27 = -27
blocks.answer:
The third line broke. The theorem takes F at the upper limit minus F at the lower limit, so it is F(3) minus F(0).

27 minus 0 = 27

The integral is 27.

Why it looks reasonable: the antiderivative is right, and so are both values of F. Only the order is wrong. The check that catches it: the rate 12 minus 2t is above zero all the way from 0 to 3. So its total must be above zero.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

∫ from 0 to 3 of t2 dt
raise the power by one: an antiderivative is t3
33 minus 03 = 27
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. Raising the power by one is half the rule. The other half divides by the new power. An antiderivative of t2 is t3 divided by 3.

27 divided by 3 = 9

The integral is 9.

Differentiating back catches it at once. The rate of t3 is 3 t2, not t2. The broken answer is three times too big.

Why it looks reasonable: the power went up by one, which is the part of the rule people remember. Nothing on the page is checked.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a deficit of 480 kcal/day halves every year, so k = 0.693
the total over the first 30 days = 480 times (1 minus e(-0.693 times 30)) divided by 0.693
e(-20.79) is almost 0
480 divided by 0.693 = 692.6
so the deficit adds up to about 693 kcal over the month
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. The rate constant is 0.693 per year, and 30 is in days. The deficit is also per day. Put everything in days first.

0.693 divided by 365 = 0.001899
0.001899 times 30 = 0.05697

On the calculator, e(-0.05697) is 0.9446.

1 minus 0.9446 = 0.0554
480 times 0.0554 = 26.592
26.592 divided by 0.001899 = 14003.2

About 14,000 kilocalories over the month. A steady 480 a day would give 14,400, so the shrinking barely shows yet.

Why it looks reasonable: the formula is the right one, and each line after the second is correct arithmetic. But a total of 693 kilocalories over a month is less than two days of the starting deficit. A deficit that halves over a year cannot have shrunk that fast.

blocks.prompt:
A patient information leaflet says this. The wording is made up for this problem.

Your deficit gets smaller as you lose weight, but it never reaches zero. So the weight loss keeps going for ever, and in the end you lose what the old calorie rule said you would.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the total a shrinking deficit adds up to over all time, against the total of a steady one.

Take a deficit D0 e(-kt) that never reaches zero. Its total from 0 to T is D0 times (1 minus e(-kT)) divided by k, and that approaches D0 divided by k. Put in the numbers from this section’s illustration: 730 megajoules a year at the start, halving each year.

730 divided by 0.693 = 1053.4

However long it runs, the total stays below 1,053.4 megajoules. The steady deficit, the old rule’s picture, passes that within a year and a half.

730 times 1.5 = 1095

So “never reaches zero” does not mean “adds up to anything”. A rate can stay above zero for ever and still have a total that stops growing.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that a real deficit shrinks as an exponential. That was an assumption, chosen to show the arithmetic. It says nothing about kilograms, which need what the lost tissue was made of. And it does not say the loss stops at a fixed date. It says the total levels off, which is a different claim.

blocks.prompt:
A journalist tells you this.

A modelling paper says the old rule overstates first-year weight loss by about 100%. So to correct any figure from the old rule, just halve it.

Hall and colleagues (Lancet 2011) do say the static rule’s first-year loss is “about 100% greater” than their model’s. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: whether the gap between a steady deficit and a shrinking one is the same at every time. Use the made-up halving deficit from this section, 730 megajoules a year at the start, halving each year. It is not the paper’s model, but it shows how such a gap behaves.

Take the shrinking total as a share of the steady total, at 1, 3 and 10 years. At 3 years, e(-2.079) is 0.125, so the shrinking total is 1053.4 times 0.875, which is 921.7. At 10 years, e(-6.93) is 0.001, so the shrinking total is 1053.4 times 0.999.

526.6 divided by 730 = 0.721
921.7 divided by 2190 = 0.421
1053.4 times 0.999 = 1052.3
730 times 10 = 7300
1052.3 divided by 7300 = 0.144

For this made-up deficit, the share falls from about 72% at one year to 42% at three years and 14% at ten. The gap grows with time. So no one factor fits every year.

What this does not establish. It does not give the paper’s own correction for any year but the first, for the one modelled man. The “about 100%” is a first-year comparison. It does not establish that halving is right even at one year for a different person or deficit. And the made-up halving deficit is not the paper’s model, so its percentages are not the paper’s.

What to say instead: the old rule’s error is not a fixed factor. It grows with time, because a shrinking deficit adds up to less and less of what a steady one would.
